title: Apple CEO John Ternus Dismisses Early Foldables as “Cheap and Crappy,” Sparks Industry Debate
body:
Apple’s senior executive John Ternus has signaled that the company remains unconvinced about the current generation of fold‑able smartphones, describing many of the early devices as feeling “kind of cheap and crappy.” The candid assessment, delivered during a recent interview with TIME, underscores Apple’s cautious approach to a market that has been dominated by Samsung and a handful of other manufacturers since the first foldable debuted in 2019. While the tech giant has not ruled out a future foldable product, Ternus’ remarks suggest that Apple is waiting for a significant leap in durability, design and user experience before committing to the form factor.

Ternus’ comments arrive at a time when the foldable segment is finally beginning to shed its prototype reputation. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold and Z Flip lines have evolved from fragile, expensive novelties to more polished, albeit still pricey, devices. Huawei, Motorola and even Microsoft have experimented with hinge mechanisms and flexible displays, but most have struggled with issues such as screen creasing, uneven weight distribution and limited software optimization. The perception of “cheapness” that Ternus highlighted reflects not only the tactile feel of early models but also the lingering concerns about long‑term reliability—a key factor for Apple’s discerning customer base.

Apple’s own product roadmap has historically been guided by a principle of “waiting for the right moment.” The company famously delayed its entry into the smartwatch market until the Apple Watch could offer a seamless blend of hardware, software and health capabilities, and it took several iterations before the iPhone’s camera system reached a level of maturity that set industry standards. In the foldable arena, Apple appears to be applying the same rigor. Industry analysts note that Apple’s supply chain partners, including Samsung Display, are already producing more robust ultra‑thin glass and polymer composites that could address the durability gap. However, integrating such materials into a consumer‑ready device demands extensive testing, a process Apple is unlikely to shortcut.

The strategic calculus behind Apple’s hesitancy also involves ecosystem considerations. Foldable phones introduce a new set of UI challenges: apps must adapt to dynamic screen sizes, and developers need tools to ensure a consistent experience across both folded and unfolded states. Apple’s ecosystem thrives on uniformity, and a fragmented foldable market could complicate the seamless interaction that iOS users expect. Ternus’ remarks may therefore be as much about the software ecosystem as they are about hardware quality. Until Apple can guarantee that its operating system will handle the fluidity of a folding display without compromising performance or battery life, the company may prefer to observe rather than to lead.

Competitors are not standing still. Samsung has recently unveiled a third‑generation hinge that promises a 30‑percent reduction in visible crease depth, while Huawei’s latest foldable claims a 20‑percent increase in screen durability through a new “nanocoating” process. These incremental improvements suggest that the technology is maturing, but the consensus among experts is that a truly premium foldable—one that matches Apple’s standards for build quality, software integration and price‑to‑value ratio—has yet to materialize. The market’s willingness to absorb higher price points will also be a decisive factor; Apple’s devices typically sit at the top of the price spectrum, and a foldable that feels “premium” must justify a premium cost.

Looking ahead, Ternus’ candid appraisal hints that Apple may be quietly conducting its own research and development, waiting for a breakthrough that would allow it to enter the foldable space without compromising its brand ethos. If Apple does decide to launch a foldable, it will likely be several years out, arriving only after the technology has proven its durability, refined its software ecosystem and achieved a price point that aligns with Apple’s value proposition. Until then, the company’s measured stance serves as a reminder that innovation at Apple is less about being first and more about being right—delivering products that feel inevitable rather than experimental.
